q: In which year did the Western Roman Empire traditionally fall?
x: In 476 the Germanic leader Odoacer deposed the teenage emperor Romulus Augustulus. The Eastern Roman Empire lasted almost another thousand years.

q: Who founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire in the 6th century BC?
x: Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BC. The Cyrus Cylinder from that time is often described as an early statement on tolerance of subject peoples.

q: From which North African city did the general Hannibal come?
x: Carthage lay near modern Tunis. Rome fought three Punic Wars against it and finally destroyed the city in 146 BC.

q: William of Normandy defeated which Anglo-Saxon king at Hastings in 1066?
x: Harold had marched his army about 250 miles in under three weeks after beating a Norwegian invasion in the north.

q: Alexander the Great was king of which kingdom?
x: Alexander took the throne at age 20 and created an empire reaching from Greece to northwestern India before dying at 32.

q: Which Spartan king led the Greek defense at Thermopylae in 480 BC?
x: Leonidas and his 300 Spartans, with several thousand allies, held a narrow pass against the huge Persian army for three days.

q: Who unified China in 221 BC and became its first emperor?
x: He standardized writing, money and measurements, and linked earlier defensive walls that became the first Great Wall.

q: Near which Chinese city was the Terracotta Army discovered in 1974?
x: Farmers digging a well found the army, which includes more than 8,000 life-size soldiers, each with a different face.

q: Mansa Musa, famed for his wealth and a 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca, ruled which empire?
x: He gave away so much gold in Cairo that the price of gold there reportedly stayed depressed for years.

q: In which year did the Suez Canal open?
x: The canal linking the Mediterranean and the Red Sea cut thousands of miles off voyages between Europe and Asia.

q: Which Portuguese explorer led the 1519 expedition that became the first to sail around the world?
x: Magellan was killed in the Philippines in 1521. Only 18 men of about 270 completed the voyage, under Juan Sebastian Elcano.

q: Which Roman emperor issued the Edict of Milan in 313, tolerating Christianity?
x: Constantine also moved the capital east, founding Constantinople in AD 330 on the site of the old city of Byzantium.

q: Which Scottish queen was executed in 1587 on the orders of Elizabeth I?
x: Mary had been held in English captivity for nearly 19 years. Her son James VI later inherited Elizabeth's throne.

q: In which year did the English defeat the Spanish Armada?
x: The English used fireships to scatter the Spanish fleet at Gravelines, and storms on the long route home destroyed many more ships.

q: Which 1648 settlement ended the Thirty Years' War?
x: Westphalia is often seen as the start of the modern system of sovereign states, and the war had devastated much of Germany.

q: Which French king was executed during the Revolution in January 1793?
x: Louis XVI had been king since 1774. His wife Marie Antoinette was executed nine months later.

q: To which Mediterranean island was Napoleon first exiled in 1814?
x: Napoleon escaped from Elba in February 1815 and returned to power for the Hundred Days, which ended at Waterloo.

q: Which British admiral won the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805 but was killed in the fighting?
x: Nelson's signal "England expects that every man will do his duty" is still famous. The victory ended Napoleon's hopes of invading Britain.

q: Which Prussian statesman engineered the unification of Germany in 1871?
x: Bismarck used three short wars against Denmark, Austria and France to build the German Empire, which was proclaimed at Versailles.

q: Which Italian patriot led the Red Shirts in the 1860 campaign to unify Italy?
x: Garibaldi conquered Sicily and Naples with about a thousand volunteers and then handed his gains to the king of Piedmont.

q: The Charge of the Light Brigade took place during which war?
x: The charge at Balaclava in 1854 resulted from a misunderstood order. Tennyson's poem made it a lasting symbol of courage.

q: Which island was ceded to Britain in 1842 after the First Opium War?
x: The Treaty of Nanking gave Britain Hong Kong Island, which stayed British until 1997, along with the opening of five Chinese ports to trade.

q: Which event of 1868 ended the Tokugawa shogunate and returned power to the Japanese emperor?
x: Japan then modernized at remarkable speed, building railways, a modern army and an industrial economy within a few decades.

q: Which US naval officer's 1853 arrival in Tokyo Bay pressured Japan to open to trade?
x: Perry's "black ships" were steam-powered, which astonished the Japanese. He returned in 1854 and signed a treaty.

q: In 1857 soldiers called sepoys rebelled in India against the rule of which company?
x: After the rebellion, Britain dissolved the company and began ruling India directly under the Crown in 1858.

q: What was the late-1800s race by European powers to claim African territory called?
x: By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent. The Berlin Conference of 1884-85 set ground rules among the colonial powers.

q: At which naval battle in 31 BC did Octavian win the war that made him sole ruler of Rome?
x: The victory off western Greece led to Octavian becoming Augustus, and Egypt then became a Roman province.

q: Which Persian king invaded Greece in 480 BC with a vast army and fleet?
x: Xerxes reportedly had a bridge of boats built across the Hellespont. His army burned Athens but his fleet lost at Salamis.

q: Which statesman led Athens during its golden age and oversaw the building of the Parthenon?
x: Pericles guided Athens for about 30 years until a plague killed him in 429 BC during the Peloponnesian War.

q: Which philosopher, a student of Socrates, founded the Academy in Athens?
x: Plato's Academy, founded around 387 BC, operated for centuries and is often called the first university in the Western world.

q: Which French scholar deciphered Egyptian hieroglyphs in 1822?
x: Champollion used the Rosetta Stone, which carries the same decree in hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek, and realized the signs recorded sounds.

q: Which female pharaoh built a famous mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari?
x: Hatshepsut ruled for about two decades in the 15th century BC and sent a famous trading expedition to the land of Punt.

q: Which pharaoh had the great temples of Abu Simbel carved into a cliff?
x: In the 1960s the temples were cut apart and moved uphill to save them from the rising waters of Lake Nasser.

q: For which pharaoh was the Great Pyramid of Giza built?
x: Khufu's pyramid held about 2.3 million stone blocks. The Greeks later called him Cheops.

q: Which Babylonian king issued a famous law code around 1750 BC?
x: The code was carved on a tall black stone slab, now in the Louvre, and includes the principle of "an eye for an eye."

q: Which people of ancient Mesopotamia developed cuneiform writing?
x: Cuneiform began around 3400 BC as pictures pressed into wet clay with a reed stylus, originally to keep trade records.

q: Which grandson of Genghis Khan founded China's Yuan dynasty?
x: Kublai completed the conquest of Song China in 1279 and moved his capital to what is now Beijing.

q: Which Chinese admiral led giant treasure fleets across the Indian Ocean in the early 1400s?
x: His voyages reached East Africa and were larger than any European fleet of the time, but China halted them after his death.

q: In which year did the Ottomans capture Constantinople?
x: Sultan Mehmed II was just 21. The Ottomans used enormous cannons to breach the city's ancient walls, ending the Byzantine Empire.

q: Which English king won the Battle of Agincourt in 1415?
x: English longbowmen helped Henry's much smaller army defeat the French on a muddy field during the Hundred Years' War.

q: Which English king was killed at the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485?
x: His death ended the Wars of the Roses and began the Tudor dynasty. His skeleton was found under a car park in Leicester in 2012.

q: Which 1534 act made the English monarch head of the Church of England?
x: Henry VIII pushed it through after the pope refused to annul his marriage to Catherine of Aragon.

q: Which Polish astronomer proposed a Sun-centered model of the universe in 1543?
x: His book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres was published as he lay near death in 1543.

q: Which conquistador captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa in 1532?
x: Pizarro's small force of fewer than 200 men took the emperor prisoner at Cajamarca and then collected a huge ransom of gold.

q: Columbus's 1492 fleet consisted of the Santa Maria, the Pinta and which other ship?
x: The Santa Maria ran aground off Hispaniola on Christmas Day 1492, and its timbers were used to build a fort.

q: On which ship did Francis Drake sail around the world between 1577 and 1580?
x: Drake returned laden with Spanish treasure and was knighted aboard his ship by Elizabeth I in 1581.

q: Which British navigator charted the east coast of Australia in 1770?
x: Cook's ship Endeavour was nearly lost on the Great Barrier Reef, and he claimed the coast for Britain as New South Wales.

q: Which Scottish missionary-explorer was famously found by Henry Morton Stanley in 1871?
x: Stanley is said to have greeted him with "Dr. Livingstone, I presume?" Livingstone had not been heard from in years.

q: Who led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in December 1911?
x: Amundsen's Norwegian team used sled dogs and beat Scott's British party by about five weeks.

q: Which Shoshone woman guided the Lewis and Clark expedition?
x: She joined the journey while carrying her infant son. Her presence helped signal peaceful intentions to other nations.

q: The 1848 discovery of gold at Sutter's Mill set off a rush to which region?
x: By 1849 tens of thousands of "forty-niners" had poured in, and San Francisco grew from a village into a major city.

q: In which state was the Battle of Gettysburg fought in July 1863?
x: The three-day battle was the bloodiest of the Civil War. Lincoln spoke at the cemetery four months later.

q: In which year did Lincoln issue the Emancipation Proclamation?
x: It took effect on January 1, 1863, declaring enslaved people in Confederate-held territory free. The 13th Amendment ended slavery nationwide in 1865.

q: In which US state did the first transcontinental railroad join up at Promontory Summit in 1869?
x: A ceremonial golden spike marked the meeting of the Central Pacific and Union Pacific lines, cutting cross-country travel from months to days.

q: In which year was the Treaty of Versailles signed?
x: It was signed on June 28, 1919, exactly five years after the assassination in Sarajevo, and required Germany to pay reparations.

q: In which year was the Battle of the Somme fought?
x: On the first day, July 1, 1916, the British Army suffered about 57,000 casualties, its worst single day.

q: Which British ocean liner was sunk by a German U-boat in 1915?
x: The sinking off Ireland killed nearly 1,200 people, including 128 Americans, and turned US public opinion against Germany.

q: Who founded the Republic of Turkey in 1923?
x: The surname Ataturk, meaning "father of the Turks," was given to him in 1934. He also replaced the Arabic script with a Latin-based alphabet.

q: In which year did India gain independence from Britain?
x: At independence in August 1947 the subcontinent was divided into India and Pakistan, in one of history's largest migrations.

q: Which general led the Nationalist side to victory in the Spanish Civil War?
x: The war lasted from 1936 to 1939, and Franco ruled Spain until his death in 1975.

q: Which city's 1942-43 battle ended with the surrender of Germany's 6th Army?
x: The battle is often called the turning point on the Eastern Front. The city is now called Volgograd.

q: From which French port were over 330,000 Allied troops evacuated in May and June 1940?
x: Hundreds of small civilian boats joined navy ships in the rescue, which Churchill called "a miracle of deliverance."

q: What was the code name of the US project that built the first atomic bombs?
x: The project employed over 100,000 people, with major sites at Los Alamos, Oak Ridge and Hanford, and the first test came in July 1945.

q: In which German city were leading Nazis tried after World War II?
x: The Nuremberg trials began in November 1945 and helped set precedents for international law on war crimes.

q: Which US Secretary of State gave his name to the 1948 plan to rebuild Western Europe?
x: The plan sent about 13 billion dollars in aid, and Marshall received the 1953 Nobel Peace Prize.

q: In which year was NATO founded?
x: Twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington in April 1949, promising to treat an attack on one as an attack on all.

q: Which line of latitude divided Korea into two zones in 1945?
x: Two young US officers chose the line in a matter of minutes using a National Geographic map.

q: Which Soviet leader agreed to withdraw missiles from Cuba in 1962?
x: The 13-day standoff ended when the US secretly agreed to remove its own missiles from Turkey and pledged not to invade Cuba.

q: Who became the first woman in space in 1963?
x: Tereshkova orbited Earth 48 times in Vostok 6. The next woman in space did not follow until 1982.

q: Who became the first American in space in May 1961?
x: Shepard's suborbital flight lasted only about 15 minutes. Ten years later he walked on the Moon on Apollo 14.

q: In which year was the Berlin Wall built?
x: East Germany put up barbed wire and then concrete overnight on August 13, 1961 to stop its citizens from fleeing to the West.

q: In which year was the Soviet Union dissolved?
x: It ended on December 26, 1991, after Mikhail Gorbachev resigned and fifteen republics became independent countries.

q: Which Scottish engineer greatly improved the steam engine in the 1760s and 1770s?
x: The unit of power, the watt, is named after him. He also introduced the term "horsepower."

q: Which English engineer built the locomotive Rocket, which won a famous trial in 1829?
x: Rocket reached about 30 miles per hour and helped prove steam locomotives could run passenger railways.

q: Who invented the cotton gin in 1793?
x: The machine made cleaning cotton far faster, which dramatically expanded cotton farming and, tragically, slavery in the American South.

q: Which American developed the electric telegraph and a code of dots and dashes?
x: The first official message, sent in 1844 from Washington to Baltimore, was "What hath God wrought."

q: On which ship did Charles Darwin sail around the world from 1831 to 1836?
x: The voyage took Darwin to the Galapagos Islands, where his observations of finches helped shape his theory of evolution.

q: Which British MP led the long campaign that ended the slave trade in the British Empire in 1807?
x: Wilberforce lived to hear that the Slavery Abolition Act, which freed slaves across the empire, was passing in 1833.

q: Who led the Haitian Revolution, which began in 1791?
x: Haiti became independent in 1804 and was the first republic led by formerly enslaved people.

q: Which Venezuelan-born leader helped liberate Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia from Spain?
x: Bolivia is named in his honor, and he was often called El Libertador.

q: Which Zulu king built a powerful military state in southern Africa in the early 1800s?
x: Shaka reorganized his army, introducing a short stabbing spear and the "buffalo horns" formation.

q: Which African country defeated an Italian invasion force at the Battle of Adwa in 1896?
x: Emperor Menelik II's victory kept Ethiopia independent and made it a symbol of resistance to colonialism.

q: The 1911 revolution in China ended the rule of which dynasty?
x: The last emperor, Puyi, was a child of six. The Qing had ruled since 1644, and the Republic of China was proclaimed in 1912.

q: William the Conqueror ordered which great survey of England, completed in 1086?
x: The survey recorded who owned land, livestock and mills in nearly every English village, and gave the king a detailed picture of his wealth.

q: Which Frankish king was crowned Emperor by the pope on Christmas Day in 800?
x: Charlemagne ruled much of Western Europe and promoted learning, helping spark a revival now called the Carolingian Renaissance.

q: Which Russian tsar founded the city of St. Petersburg in 1703?
x: Peter built it on marshland as a "window to the West," and it served as Russia's capital for over 200 years.

q: At which Virginia town did British General Cornwallis surrender in 1781?
x: A French fleet trapped Cornwallis from the sea while Washington's and Rochambeau's armies surrounded him by land.

q: In 1814, British troops burned public buildings in which American city?
x: The burning of the White House and Capitol happened during the War of 1812. A rainstorm helped put out the fires.

q: In which year did the 19th Amendment guarantee American women the right to vote?
x: The amendment was ratified in August 1920 after about 72 years of campaigning that began at the Seneca Falls convention in 1848.

q: Which British suffragette leader founded the Women's Social and Political Union in 1903?
x: The group's motto was "Deeds, not words." British women over 30 gained the vote in 1918, a decade before full equality.

q: Which Mughal emperor built the Taj Mahal in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal?
x: Construction took about 20 years from the 1630s, and the white marble mausoleum is said to have involved some 20,000 workers.

q: Mesopotamia, the cradle of early civilization, lay between the Tigris and which other river?
x: The name Mesopotamia means "between the rivers" in Greek, and the region included the first cities such as Ur and Uruk.

q: Which Chinese dynasty followed the short-lived Qin and ruled for about four centuries?
x: Under the Han, the Silk Road opened and paper was invented. The majority ethnic group of China still calls itself "Han."

q: In which year did the Gunpowder Plot to blow up the English Parliament take place?
x: Guy Fawkes was caught guarding 36 barrels of gunpowder beneath the House of Lords, and Britons still mark Bonfire Night each November 5.

q: Which Chinese dynasty built the Forbidden City in Beijing in the early 1400s?
x: Construction began in 1406 under the Yongle Emperor. The palace complex has nearly 1,000 buildings and housed 24 emperors.

q: Which US president signed the Civil Rights Act of 1964?
x: Johnson signed it on July 2, 1964, outlawing discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin.

q: Who was Emperor of Japan during World War II?
x: Hirohito reigned from 1926 to 1989, the longest of any Japanese emperor, and his radio address announced Japan's surrender in 1945.

q: Who became India's first female Prime Minister, in 1966?
x: She was the daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first Prime Minister, and she served until 1977 and again from 1980 to 1984.

q: Which Carthaginian general famously crossed the Alps with elephants?
x: Hannibal marched into Italy in 218 BC during the Second Punic War.

q: Which treaty formally ended World War I with Germany in 1919?
x: The treaty was signed in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles.
